t: LeetCode 1815 - Maximum Number of Groups Getting Fresh Donuts: Remainders, Blocks and Memoized DP
o: Only each group size modulo batchSize matters: a group is happy exactly when the donut counter sits at a batch boundary when it arrives, meaning the sum of all previously served group sizes is divisible by batchSize. An arrangement therefore splits into consecutive zero-sum blocks plus a possibly ragged tail, and maximizing happy groups is maximizing block starts. In example 1 (batchSize 3, mods 0,0,1,1,2,2) the order [6,2,4,5,1,3] forms blocks [6], [2,4], [5,1], [3] - four happy groups, since only the first group of each block starts fresh. The constraints scream compression: batchSize <= 9 gives eight nonzero residue classes and there are at most 30 groups, so a memoized search over residue-count vectors with the running remainder as part of the state is entirely feasible.
k: Reduce every group to g mod batchSize; groups with remainder 0 are happy no matter where they are placed.
Happy groups equal the number of times the running sum hits 0 mod batchSize - one per zero-sum block.
Complementary remainders r and batchSize - r concatenate into ready-made zero blocks and can be paired greedily.
The leftover multiset after pairing is tiny (batchSize <= 9), so DP over residue counts finishes instantly.

a.i: Strip multiples of batchSize (each contributes one guaranteed happy group). Then build the arrangement residue by residue: the state is how many groups of each nonzero remainder remain, plus the current running remainder mod batchSize. Placing a group of remainder i when the running remainder is 0 earns a happiness point; memoize on (counts, remainder). Correct by construction, though its state space can be large before any pruning.
s: Count freq[r] for each residue r; add freq[0] to the answer
DFS(counts, rem): try every remaining residue i next
Recurse with counts minus one i and rem = (rem + i) mod batchSize
Add 1 to the candidate when rem was 0 before placing
Memoize on (counts tuple, rem); answer = base + DFS
a.t: O(b x P) where P is the product of (freq[r] + 1) over nonzero residues - exponential in theory but tiny given batchSize <= 9 and <= 30 groups.
a.sp: O(P x b) memo entries of size-b count vectors.

a.n: Approach 2: Greedy Pairing Plus DP on Leftovers
a.i: Before any search, harvest structure: a group of remainder r followed by one of remainder batchSize - r sums to a full batch, so each complementary pair is a self-contained zero block worth exactly one happy group; pair them greedily (the middle remainder b/2 pairs with itself when b is even). Only unpaired leftovers - a very small multiset - need the memoized search from Approach 1, which collapses the state space dramatically.
s: Tally residues; answer starts at freq[0]
For r and batchSize - r, add min(freq[r], freq[batchSize - r]) pairs; for r = b/2 add floor(freq[r]/2)
Run the same memoized DFS over what remains
Return greedy total plus DFS result
a.t: O(b x P) again but P now ranges over leftover counts only - near-instant in practice.
a.sp: O(P x b) for the memo on leftovers.

w: Open with the remainder reduction and the block interpretation - that framing earns the design points - then code Approach 1 and upgrade it to Approach 2 live. Pitfalls: crediting every member of a zero block instead of just its first group, forgetting the self-pairing case when batchSize is even, and adding the +1 bonus after the recursion instead of guarding it on entering with rem == 0. Follow-ups: reconstruct an optimal ordering by storing the chosen residue per state; handle customers who leave angry (groups must all be fresh) by counting only complete blocks.
